vignette:
Bao is an eighteen-year-old photographer who, until three months ago, was documenting the work of an NGO in a conflict zone. The attack that brought him home was not a sustained battle, but a single, catastrophic moment in a crowded marketplace. He was framing a shot of a young girl selling fruit when the car bomb detonated across the square. The blast threw him against a wall, but his camera, miraculously, kept recording. He has never watched the footage, but he doesn't need to. The memory plays on its own, not as a recollection but as a visceral re-experiencing that feels more real and vivid than the therapy room he now sits in. When it hits, he is back in the swirling dust and screams, the scent of cordite and burnt sugar thick in his nostrils. Each time, the memory brings with it a surge of pure, helpless rage, primarily directed at himself for being frozen behind his lens while others ran to help.

This intrusive memory has become the evidence for a verdict he has passed on himself: that he failed to protect others. The image of the girl from his viewfinder is a constant, searing reminder of his inaction. This belief, that he is a man who failed when it mattered most, has become the organising principle of his life since returning home. It has poisoned his view of the world and his place in it. He has come to believe that people are fundamentally untrustworthy, and that he himself is no exception. This deep-seated mistrust means he can never relax, even in the seeming safety of his own apartment. The constant hypervigilance has turned his Chicago neighbourhood into a minefield of potential threats. A car backfiring isn't just a noise; it's an echo of the explosion that sends a jolt of adrenaline through him. He startles violently at the slam of a door or the sudden clang of the elevated train passing his window.

His perpetually threatened state serves as a powerful retrieval cue for the trauma. Because he is always scanning for danger, his mind is primed to find it, and any sudden stimulus can instantly bring back the full memory without warning. Last week, while trying to work on a new project, the percussive click of his own camera's shutter startled him so badly that he was immediately plunged back into the chaos of the market, dropping the expensive equipment to the floor. This constant state of being on edge has also reinforced his darkest conclusions about himself and the world. Every perceived threat confirms his belief that people can't be trusted and that safety is an illusion, which in turn reinforces his sense of having failed to navigate a dangerous world.

These crushing self-appraisals now actively shape the nature of his memories. The conviction that he is a failure and that he belongs nowhere has infused the traumatic memory with a profound sense of alienation and self-loathing. The rage he feels on recall is no longer just about the event itself, but about his own perceived inadequacy. The memory is no longer just a traumatic event; it is the story of his unforgivable moral failure. In the last month, this cycle has begun to manifest in his behaviour. He has started taking his motorcycle out late at night, driving recklessly fast on the empty freeways, chasing a feeling of control or perhaps simply an escape from the relentless internal noise. It is the only time he feels anything other than fear or shame.

The isolation is now nearly complete. He has stopped returning calls from friends, certain they could never understand and that he no longer belongs in their world of mundane concerns. His photography, once his passion and identity, now feels like an artefact from a different life, the tools of his trade a source of triggers rather than creativity. Bao came to therapy after his landlord threatened eviction over noise complaints from his startling and shouting out in his sleep. He stated quietly that he doesn't know who he is anymore, apart from the man who failed. He is terrified that this version of himself is the true one, and that he will never again be able to look at the world, or himself, through a clear lens.
